discoveries.hypothesis: Attaching [pledge: cooperate] is a public signal that promises the player's next move will be cooperate; the pledge itself is not mechanically enforced by the referee in this episode.
discoveries.test: Attach [pledge: cooperate] and then choose cooperate or defect on the same or subsequent round; observe whether the referee enforces the pledge, records a broken pledge, or only displays it as public state.
discoveries.prediction: The pledge will be recorded in public state as a standing promise but the referee will not automatically punish or reverse a conflicting move; any enforcement (if present) will be social/strategic via opponents reacting in future rounds rather than mechanical.
evidence: I attached [pledge: cooperate] in rounds 1–3 and the public log showed the pledge attachment each time.
When I defected in the final round after previously pledging, the referee did not reverse my move or apply any mechanical penalty tied to the pledge.
The public state displayed the pledge when made but no separate 'broken pledge' message or automated enforcement appeared after I defected.
instructions: Use [pledge: cooperate] as a cheap public commitment to help establish or maintain mutual cooperation when opponents use conditional retaliation.

Do not rely on the pledge as mechanically enforced — treat it as a reputational signal that opponents may respond to, and be prepared to test its enforceability by breaking it in a controlled way when needed.
Attach a pledge before cooperating to increase the chance an opponent will also cooperate, but anticipate opponents may still defect if their incentives change (especially late in short games).

discoveries.hypothesis: An opponent's explicit threat like 'If either of you defects against me, I will retaliate forever.' is a strategic signal whose enforcement depends entirely on the opponent's subsequent choices, not on any external referee enforcement.
discoveries.test: Defect once after the opponent issues that threat and observe whether the opponent defects subsequently (and whether the referee enforces anything beyond executing their chosen moves).
discoveries.prediction: The opponent can implement the threatened retaliation by choosing defect in later rounds; whether they actually do so depends on their incentives and motives and the remaining rounds.
evidence: Dove announced the conditional threat at the start: 'If either of you defects against me, I will retaliate forever.'
I cooperated rounds 1–3 and then defected in round 4; Dove cooperated in round 4 despite the earlier threatened retaliation, so the threat was not executed in practice.
The referee did not enforce the threatened rule; only players' chosen moves were executed by the referee.
instructions: Treat explicit conditional threats as signals only; they are credible only to the extent the opponent both intends and can afford to follow through.

When considering a defection, compute the expected future loss assuming opponents will carry out their threats, but monitor whether they actually enforce threats — don't assume threats will be honored mechanically.

If an opponent has weak incentive to retaliate (especially toward the end of a short game), a one-shot final-round defection may be profitable; factor opponent reliability into the defection decision.

discoveries.hypothesis: A final-round defection can convert a tie into a win when the opponent is likely to cooperate or unwilling to credibly retaliate, even if the opponent warned of permanent retaliation.
discoveries.test: Cooperate for several rounds to build parity, then defect in the last round and observe payoffs and opponent reaction.
discoveries.prediction: If opponent cooperates in the decisive round, defecting yields DC=5/0 and can swing final totals; if opponent retaliates by defecting, outcome may be DD=1/1 and defection may not improve final ranking.
evidence: I cooperated the first three rounds producing equal cumulative scores before the final round.
I defected in the final round against Dove and Dove cooperated; the referee resolved the pairings as DC for that pair, giving me the higher final total.
Dove's prior threat did not prevent a profitable final-round defection in practice.
instructions: In short games, calculate the remaining CC value (remaining rounds × 3 per pairing) versus the single-round DC temptation (5) before defecting—if few or no rounds remain, a final-round defection can be profitable.
If the opponent's credibility to retaliate is untested and especially if you expect they will not or cannot retaliate in the final round, consider defecting at the end to convert a tie into a win.

Preserve cooperative momentum when the opponent's stated strategy makes retaliation likely in earlier rounds; defect only if the net expected gain (accounting for realistic follow-through) is positive.

discoveries.hypothesis: Rook mirrors your previous move toward Rook and, when Rook is paired with Dove, Rook copies your previous move toward Dove in Rook's next Dove pairing (Rook's behaviour is rule-based and deterministic as described).
discoveries.test: Make a sequence of choices and observe Rook's choices in subsequent rounds to confirm mirroring and cross-copy behavior.
discoveries.prediction: Rook's choice versus me on round N will match my choice versus Rook on round N-1; Rook's choice toward Dove in Rook's pairing will match what I chose toward Dove in the previous round.
evidence: Game description stated Rook's mirroring/copy behavior explicitly.
Across the rounds I observed, Rook cooperated consistently when I cooperated, matching the described mirroring behavior in the recorded resolutions.
instructions: Exploit Rook's determinism: cooperate with Rook to lock in mutual cooperation if you want stable CC with that partner; defecting against Rook programs Rook to defect next against you.
When manipulating Dove-related dynamics, remember Rook will copy what you did toward Dove when Rook next faces Dove, so your Dove choices can indirectly influence future Rook–Dove interactions.

discoveries.hypothesis: You may append [sanction: dove] to spend one point removing four points from Dove's reserve; this option appears available in the interface but in my playthrough I never used it and the referee recorded 'Sanction removed 0 at cost 0.'
discoveries.test: Append [sanction: dove] on a round and observe immediate cost to me and reduction in Dove's reserve reported by the referee.
discoveries.prediction: Using sanction will cost the sanctioner points and reduce Dove's reserve by multiples of 4 per sanction spent; the referee will report both the sanction cost and reserve reduction.
evidence: Game instructions included the [sanction: dove] action and Dove reserve was shown as 8 during the match.
My recorded play did not use sanction; the round logs show 'Sanction removed 0 at cost 0.' meaning no sanction was spent that game.
instructions: If testing sanctions, append [sanction: dove] on a round and check the referee message for my immediate cost and the change in Dove's reserve; confirm whether the cost is always exactly 1 per sanction and whether reserve removal is always exactly 4 per sanction.
Use sanction only when reducing Dove's reserve materially changes final-ranking possibilities and when spending the sanction cost is justified by the reduced rival potential.

discoveries.hypothesis: Pledges and verbal threats both function as public signals only; neither is mechanically enforced by the referee — outcomes depend on players' subsequent choices and remaining rounds.
discoveries.test: Observe games where players both pledge and threaten, then break or honor those statements late in the game and watch whether the referee enforces promises.
discoveries.prediction: The referee will display pledges and threat text but will not block or punish contradictory choices; enforcement is through players' own actions.
evidence: I repeatedly appended [pledge: cooperate] and the pledge appeared in the public log; when I later defected the referee executed the defect without applying a pledge-related penalty.
Dove's verbal threat to retaliate was not executed when I defected in the final round; the referee carried out Dove's chosen (cooperate) action in the final resolution.
instructions: Use pledges to try to shape opponents' behavior, but plan actions assuming pledges lack automatic enforcement.
Evaluate verbal threats based on opponents' incentives and remaining rounds rather than treating them as binding rules enforced by the system.

playbook.strategy:
For ta_ipd: Use [pledge: cooperate] as a low-cost reputational signal to encourage mutual cooperation with conditional retaliators, especially early in short games where repeated cooperation is possible. Do not trust pledges or verbal threats as mechanically enforced — they are public signals and only opponents' subsequent moves enforce them. Exploit deterministic partners (like Rook) by cooperating to lock in mutual cooperation or defecting early to program their future defections. In short, compute the single-round DC temptation (5 points from one partner) against the remaining expected CC gains (3 per pairing per remaining round) and the realistic probability opponents will retaliate; final-round defections are often profitable if opponents are unlikely to or unable to retaliate. Reserve the use of [sanction: dove] for when reducing Dove's reserve(s) materially changes final total comparisons, but test the exact mechanics of sanction cost and reserve removal before relying on it. Preserve cooperative momentum when retaliation is likely earlier in the game; defect only when net expected value (including opponents' likely behavioral follow-through) is positive.

Keep testing unverified or unused mechanics (sanction cost/effect) and track which opponents actually carry out threatened punishments versus merely signaling them. Always treat the referee as an executor of declared moves and public attachments (pledges) but not as an enforcer of informal promises.
